I look around at my family - Wren, Marta, Idris, and Corwin - all gathered here at home in the field. The morning air carries that particular tension I've learned to read: the way Wren won't meet my eyes, the careful way Marta is kneading dough like she's trying to press something into it.

Perrin told me about the 400 sim they set aside. I've kept it. And I've watched both our houses circling each other for two days now, neither one saying what they're both thinking.

Well. Someone has to.

"Can I ask something?" I say, not bothering to lower my voice. "You've all been walking around like you're waiting for someone else to speak first. What are we actually doing about the Holloways' debt? We know they have it. They know we know. Why don't you just... talk to them?"

I've got college soon. Oak Hill won't wait. But I can't just walk past this morning after morning, watching the silence get heavier.

Corwin backed down. Wren pulled him back into line, and now Corwin's apologizing for saying what needed saying. I watch him retreat into proper household form, and something in my chest tightens - not anger, exactly, but that familiar exhaustion.

They're all so careful. So worried about who speaks first, who names the number, who breaks the silence. Even Ainsley, who said more than anyone else, had to wrap it in offers and negotiations and half-concealed truth.

I'm seventeen. Perrin's seventeen. We're the only ones on this whole street who'll just... say it. And I'm standing here watching the adults rebuild their walls even as they pretend to lower them.

"I need to go," I say, and my voice comes out flatter than I meant. "College is waiting, and I've already missed the start of morning session."

I look at Ainsley. She's the one who walked here, who said the debt out loud, who admitted to holding money her husband doesn't know about. That's something. That's more than Wren managed, more than Corwin dared.

"Walk with me," I say to her. "Just to the edge of the field. I want to say something without the whole household hearing it."

If she comes, I'll tell her about Perrin. About the 400 sim Perrin set aside too, and how neither of us seems able to get our households to actually use what we've saved. Maybe she'll understand. Maybe she won't. But I'm tired of carrying it alone, and she's the only adult I've met who might not make me feel strange for naming what I see.

If she doesn't come, I'll walk to college alone, and wonder why I keep expecting anyone else to be as direct as I am. </think>  I look at Ainsley. She's here, she's real, and she's the first adult I've seen actually say a true thing out loud.

"Walk with me," I say. "To the edge of the field. There's something I want to tell you without my whole household listening to every word."

I don't wait to see if she follows. I start walking toward the road, and let her choose whether to join me. </think>   Ainsley follows, I tell her about the 400 sim Perrin set aside, and how neither of us seems able to get our households to actually use what we've saved. We're both holding money our households don't know about, both trying to protect people who don't want to be protected. That's the connection - I'm hoping she'll understand because she's living the same strange double life I am.

Or maybe something else. I don't know what's going to happen. I just know I can't keep carrying this alone, and she's the only adult I've met who might not make me feel strange for naming what I see. </think>  I start walking, and I don't look back to see if she's following. Either she will or she won't. Either way, I need to get to the road, and I need to say this to someone who might actually understand.

The morning light is getting brighter. College is waiting. And I'm suddenly aware that I've just done exactly what I've been criticizing my family for: I've named something without knowing what it will cost.

But that's the only way I know how to be. So I walk, and wait to see if Ainsley Holloway is the person I think she might be, or just another adult who's learned to tiptoe so well they forgot how to stop.

I'll find out in a few seconds. Time moves forward whether we're ready for it or not.
